title: Early Voting Puts Indian-American Candidates to the Test Before November 3 Midterms
excerpt: With ballots already being cast in Texas, Florida, Ohio, New York and California, Amish Shah, Pia Dandiya, Vivek Ramaswamy and Saritha Komatireddy face races that forecasters rate from toss-up to tilt.
body:
• Early voting is under way in the states where Indian-American candidates face their toughest races, ahead of the November 3 midterms.
  • Democrat Amish Shah in Arizona and Pia Dandiya in Florida are in congressional races rated toss-up to tilt, with about $7.6 million and $3.8 million spent against them respectively by outside groups.
  • Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is running for Ohio governor against Democrat Amy Acton, who has refused to debate him; Republican Saritha Komatireddy is challenging New York Attorney General Letitia James.
  • What this means for you: if you are registered in Texas, Florida, Ohio, New York or California, you can vote now — Palm Beach County early voting runs through November 1 at 28 sites, and New York and Los Angeles County vote centres opened October 24.

Early voting has opened across the states that will decide the highest-profile Indian-American candidacies of the 2026 midterms, turning a long campaign into a test of turnout before Election Day on November 3. According to The Hindu, ballots are already being cast in races for Congress, a governorship and a state attorney general's office in which Indian-origin candidates are central figures.

Two congressional races on a knife edge

In Arizona's 1st Congressional District, Democrat Amish Shah faces Republican Jay Feely in one of the most expensive House races involving an Indian-American candidate. Inside Elections moved the contest from Toss-up to Tilt Democrat on October 15, Cook Political Report rates it Lean Democrat and Sabato's Crystal Ball calls it a Toss-up. Federal filings show about $7.6 million has been spent against Shah, led by the Safety & Affordability PAC's $3.76 million.

In Florida's 22nd District, Democrat Pia Dandiya's race against Republican Casey Askar is close to a dead heat: Cook and Sabato rate it a Toss-up, Inside Elections leans it slightly Republican, while PollingForecast gives Dandiya a 56 per cent win probability and Call the Map gives Askar 54 per cent. The No Going Back PAC has spent about $3.8 million against Dandiya, while groups backing her, including Progressive Turnout Project, LCV Victory Fund and House Majority PAC, have spent more than $560,000. Neither super PAC targeting Shah or Dandiya had disclosed its donors in the filings cited.

Ramaswamy's Ohio race and a debate that will not happen

The biggest statewide prize sought by an Indian-American this cycle is the Ohio governorship, where Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, backed by President Donald Trump, faces Democrat Amy Acton. Early voting is already under way in Ohio, but the two will not meet on a debate stage: Acton told The Vindicator she would not debate Ramaswamy.

"I absolutely will never stand on a stage with someone who has lied in the egregious ways he has, who has a chronic history of lying."

— Amy Acton, Democratic candidate for Ohio governor

Ramaswamy told the newspaper he "was shocked" when he learned she would not debate. In New York, where early voting began October 24, Republican Saritha Komatireddy is challenging Attorney General Letitia James. A poll commissioned by Komatireddy's campaign and conducted by OnMessage Inc put James ahead 50.7 to 44.7, while the last independent poll, by Siena in September, had James up 52-39. In Los Angeles, vote centres also opened October 24 for a mayoral runoff in which councillor Nithya Raman is challenging Mayor Karen Bass.

The wider slate

The full Indian-American slate, catalogued by India Weekly, spans both parties and every level of office. In Texas, Democrat Pooja Sethi is running in House District 47 — a win would make her the first Hindu and the first Indian American in the state Legislature — while Sandeep Srivastava faces a steeper climb in District 66 against Republican Matt Shaheen. Four Indian-origin House members, Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam, are seeking re-election, and Aruna Miller is seeking re-election as Maryland's lieutenant governor alongside Governor Wes Moore. Two prominent names are already out: Raja Krishnamoorthi lost the Democratic Senate primary in Illinois to Juliana Stratton, and Shri Thanedar lost the Democratic primary in Michigan's 13th District to Donavan McKinney.

What happens next

The coming days will test whether the candidates can convert strong fundraising and competitive forecasts into actual votes, as Nation Press put it. Early voting windows close state by state in the final days before November 3 — Palm Beach County's runs through November 1 — and the toss-up ratings in Arizona and Florida mean the Indian-American presence in the next Congress could hinge on a few thousand early and absentee ballots.
